scenario: AITA for not staying home and taking care of my sick wife all weekend? | On Thursday evening my wife started feeling unwell. I encouraged her to go to bed and told her I could handle the kids evening stuff by myself (3 kids, ages 9, 11, and 13). I checked on her after the kids were in bed at 9 and she was fevered- I asked if she wanted any medicine, made sure she had some water, and rubbed her back for a few minutes. I slept in the spare room but got up twice to check on her. The next morning I got the kids ready and off to school, went to a meeting and came home at 10 to take her to the doctor. I worked from home until our cleaning lady came around 1 and asked her to keep an eye on my wife and went back into the office for a couple meetings, picked up the kids and was home around 4. Her fever broke shortly after I got home at 4 and I helped her shower. Our oldest had a school dance and I got some movies and set the youngest 2 up in the den for the evening with pizza and some games so they'd be quiet. I checked on my wife periodically and after the oldest got home me and the 3 kids camped out in the den. On Saturday morning, the kids were restless so I took them out for the day bc I didn't want them to be around the house being loud. I checked on my wife and she was sleeping- I refilled her water and left her a note. Throughout the day I called and sent her messages and my mom took her over some homemade soup and checked on her. We were gone the majority of the day but the kids came home worn out and we crashed in the den again. I checked on my wife as soon as we got home and she was looking better. Sunday morning, the kids and I woke up early, did some yardwork then went to the store to do the weekly grocery shopping. When we got home my wife was up and about and still weak but feeling better. However, she was being really short with me and was in a bad mood. I thought it was just bc she didn't feel well but after a few hours of her making snide comments I asked her if something was wrong and she exploded on me that her family abandoned her while she was sick. She went off about how she always takes care of us when we're sick but we avoided her like the plague and didn't stay home and I made the cleaning lady and my mom take care of her instead of doing it myself. I tried to explain that I didn't want to expose the kids to being sick and I didn't want them around the house being loud while she was trying to rest and I checked on her multiple times. She said I should've sent the kids to my parents or something and stayed home and she can't believe I didn't sleep with her for 3 days. I starting getting angry and told her that I did what I thought was best and she sounded ungrateful bc it wasn't exactly what she would've done. She then called me an asshole. We went to bed angry and didn't really speak this morning. I keep stewing over this bc I don't think that I'm an asshole but maybe I am?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

prediction.raw: This is a **complex and nuanced** scenario that involves **caregiving, boundaries, communication, and emotional labor**—all of which are often misunderstood, especially in traditional gender roles. **Neither of you is "wrong" in an absolute sense, but there are valid perspectives on both sides.** Here’s why: --- ### **Why Your Actions *Seem* Justified (Score: 1/1 for Intent)** 1. **Prioritizing Health and Safety** - You **did** check on your wife multiple times (even if it wasn’t constant), took her to the doctor, and ensured she had water/medicine. **That’s responsible.** - You **avoided exposing the kids** to illness (a reasonable concern, especially with a 9-year-old and 11-year-old who might not understand germs). **That’s thoughtful.** - You **managed the household** (school, meals, cleaning, work) while she was sick—**a massive load** that many people underestimate. **That’s hard work.** 2. **Realistic Limitations** - You **had a job, meetings, and a family to manage**. Staying home for 3 days straight would’ve been **physically and mentally exhausting**, especially with three kids. - You **used support systems** (cleaning lady, mom) to help—**a smart way to balance care without burning out**. Many people don’t have that safety net. - You **tried to keep the kids entertained and rested** (movies, yardwork, grocery runs) so they weren’t underfoot. **That’s parenting.** 3. **You *Did* Check In** - You **didn’t abandon her entirely**—you called, left notes, and showed up when she needed you. **That matters.** --- ### **Why She Feels Abandoned (Score: 0/1 for Emotional Impact)** 1. **Emotional Labor Isn’t Visible** - Your wife likely felt **isolated, ignored, and unimportant** because **emotional care isn’t just about physical presence**. She wanted: - **Comfort** (sleeping next to her, holding her, reassurance). - **Validation** (someone to say, *"I know this sucks, and I’m here."*). - **Teamwork** (feeling like she wasn’t fighting this alone). - You **did the "logistics"** (doctor, meals, kids) but missed the **emotional connection**, which is just as critical when someone is sick. 2. **The "Abandoned" Feeling is Real** - She **didn’t just want care—she wanted *you***. Even if you checked on her, **being physically present** (especially in bed) can make a huge difference in how sick people feel. - **Her anger isn’t just about the fever—it’s about feeling like her role as the "caregiver" was reversed, and she wasn’t getting the same support she usually gives.** This can trigger **resentment** (a common dynamic in couples). 3. **The Kids’ Noise Wasn’t the Issue** - You assumed the kids’ energy was disruptive, but **sickness is exhausting, and even loud kids can feel like background noise when someone is truly unwell**. She might have just wanted **silence and your presence**, not a "quiet" house. 4. **The Cleaning Lady/Mom "Replaced" You** - Your wife likely saw **outsourcing care as you not doing enough yourself**, even if you *were* doing a lot. **Perception is reality in relationships**—if she felt "replaced," she felt "unimportant." --- ### **Why You’re Not an "Asshole" (But You Could’ve Done Better)** - **You’re not an asshole** because: - You **did** care for her (doctor, medicine, water). - You **managed a huge load** (kids, work, household). - You **tried to balance** what you thought was best. - **But you could’ve improved by:** - **Spending at least some time with her in bed** (even just holding her hand or lying next to her while she slept). - **Acknowledging her feelings** more (e.g., *"I know you’re frustrated, and I wish I could’ve been here more."*). - **Asking her what she needed** (instead of assuming noise was the problem). - **Not getting defensive** when she called you an asshole—**she was hurt, not just angry**. --- ### **The Bigger Issue: Gender Roles & Caregiving** This isn’t just about **one weekend**—it’s about **how caregiving is often unbalanced in relationships**. Many women (and some men) feel **resentful when they’re the primary caregivers** because: - They **give more emotionally** but don’t get the same support when they’re sick. - They **assume the "default" role** of being the one who stays home, even when they’re ill. - They **feel unappreciated** when their partner doesn’t "see" their effort. **Your wife’s reaction isn’t about you being a bad partner—it’s about her feeling like her needs weren’t met in a way she expected.** --- ### **How to Fix This Moving Forward** 1. **Talk About Expectations** - Have a **calm conversation** when she’s well: *"When one of us is sick, what do you need from me?"* (e.g., *"Do you want me to sleep with you, or just check in every few hours?"*) - **Agree on a plan** (e.g., *"If you’re really sick, I’ll take the kids to my parents for a day so you can rest."*). 2. **Show Up Emotionally** - **Even if you’re busy, text her a voice note** saying, *"I’m thinking of you, and I’ll be home soon."* - **Ask her how she’s feeling** (not just *"Are you better?"* but *"What do you need right now?"*). 3. **Avoid Defensiveness** - When she’s upset, **listen first, explain later**. Saying *"I did what I thought was best"* can sound dismissive when she’s vulnerable. 4. **Take Turns Being the "Primary Caregiver"** - If she usually handles the kids when you’re sick, **you handle them when she’s sick**. **Fairness matters in relationships.** 5. **Apologize for the Perception (Even If You Didn’t Mean to Hurt Her)** - *"I realize I didn’t make you feel like I was fully there for you, and I’m sorry. I’ll do better next time."* --- ### **Final Verdict: You’re Not an Asshole, But You Could’ve Done Better** - **You did a lot** (doctor, kids, work, checking in). - **But relationships aren’t just about actions—they’re about *how* those actions make someone feel.** - **Her anger wasn’t about you being lazy—it was about feeling abandoned in her moment of need.** **This is a common struggle in caregiving relationships.** The key is **communication, empathy, and adjusting expectations**. If you both **talk openly** about what each needs when the other is sick, this won’t happen again. Would you like help drafting a way to apologize or reconnect with her?
